rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs while limiting the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the crowded middle cluster and late doublet. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving time to use a shallower gradient if needed.

Use a threefold shallower gradient at the better-performing temperature to spread the middle cluster and test slope-dependent selectivity. The short elution window so far provides room for this change without a large time penalty.
Shorten the gradient to bring the last peak below 10 minutes while measuring how the remaining critical pair responds. The other pairs have substantial resolution margins at the 30-minute gradient.

The critical pair appears to approach an elution-order crossover as the gradient shortens from 30 to 26 minutes. Test a 20-minute gradient to seek separation on the other side of that crossover while retaining adequate resolution in the middle cluster.

Test a 5-degree temperature decrease near the best method to shift the remaining critical pair away from co-elution. Keep the gradient fixed to isolate temperature-dependent selectivity, with ample room before the 10-minute time penalty.

This gradient is slightly steeper than injection 5, targeting improved separation of its remaining critical pair while preserving the narrow resolution margin in the middle cluster. Adjusting the endpoint provides a finer slope change than shortening tG alone.

Increase the slope slightly from 0.04444 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to lift the 1.49-resolution pair above threshold while preserving the other pairs. The last peak should still elute during the gradient, so the lower endpoint should not affect its elution.

Injection 8 achieved the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Raise the starting and ending organic fractions together to test a shorter elution window at unchanged slope, checking whether the tightly resolved middle cluster remains acceptable.

Make the gradient shallower to recover the middle-cluster resolution lost at the higher starting organic fraction. This tests whether a fully resolved method can retain some of injection 9's time savings; injection 8 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Return to the successful starting fraction and test a slightly steeper slope, 0.04583 versus 0.045 organic fraction per minute. This probes whether elution can be shortened further without pushing the middle-cluster pairs below R = 1.5; injection 8 remains the benchmark.

The faster high-temperature methods have reached a tight selectivity limit, so retain injection 8 as the maximum-score benchmark. Test a lower temperature at the higher starting fraction to look for a different elution order that permits full resolution in a shorter window.

Lower temperature by one grid step to move the nearly co-eluting pair away from its apparent selectivity crossover. The other pairs at 40 C have resolution margins, and the last peak has room to shift later without a time penalty.

Test one further temperature step to separate the new middle-cluster critical pair and assess the late doublet across its apparent order crossover. Injection 8 remains the proven maximum-CRF method while this explores an alternative selectivity region.

Complete the low-temperature exploration: the shifting middle-cluster pattern suggests another 5-degree decrease may separate the remaining critical pair. The last peak is currently below 9 minutes, leaving some room before the time penalty begins.

Shorten the newly fully resolved low-temperature gradient by one grid step to reduce elution time. Check whether its critical middle and late pairs retain R ≥ 1.5, while preserving injection 8 as the faster maximum-score benchmark.

Restore the shallower slope that fully resolved the low-temperature mixture, but shift the organic window upward to shorten retention. This tests whether increased starting strength saves time without losing the critical middle-pair separation.

Test a higher organic window to move the low-temperature critical pair through its apparent elution-order crossover while shortening retention. The maximum CRF is already secured by injection 8; this explores a potentially faster fully resolved alternative.

Shift the organic window upward one more step to increase separation beyond the apparent middle-pair crossover and shorten the run. The other pairs in injection 18 have useful resolution margins, making this a promising route to a faster maximum-score method.

Injection 19 is now the fastest fully resolved method, with useful resolution margins. Shorten its gradient by one grid step to reduce retention while checking the middle cluster and late critical pair.

Shorten the gradient by another grid step to seek the fastest fully resolved method. Injection 20 retains R ≥ 1.75 throughout and remains the benchmark if the middle or late critical pair falls below 1.5.

Back off the gradient slope by lowering the endpoint one grid step, placing it between the fully resolved injection 20 and the slightly under-resolved injection 21. This should recover the critical pair while retaining some of the shorter gradient's time savings.

With the maximum CRF secured, test a higher organic window at the same slope to seek a substantially shorter fully resolved separation beyond another possible elution-order crossover. Injection 22 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.

Return to the fastest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature by one grid step to test further time savings. Check temperature-dependent selectivity carefully, retaining injection 22 if any pair falls below R = 1.5.

Return to 25 C and test a slope between injections 21 and 22 to probe the shortest fully resolved boundary. Injection 22 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method if this slightly steeper gradient leaves the critical pair below R = 1.5.
